Here is something strange about the news. Two countries read about the same event on the same morning, and by lunchtime they are having two different conversations. Nobody lied and nobody invented anything. What changed was the question each country asked about the story. One asked how much it will cost, and the other asked who decided it. Once you notice this, talking about the news with somebody from another country becomes much easier, because you stop trying to agree about the event and you start asking about the question. What did people talk about where you are? That single question has saved more international conversations than any amount of vocabulary, and it works even when you have only read the headline.

A short note about talking politics with a client abroad, because I got this wrong for years. I used to think the safe move was to say nothing at all. Then a colleague told me the opposite, and she was right. The risk is not the subject. The risk is the verdict. You can bring up almost any story in the world if you bring it as a question instead of as a conclusion. Have you been following this? What is the reaction there? People answer that happily, and they tell you what matters to them, which is the whole point of the conversation. The moment you announce what you think before anybody asked, the room gets quiet, and it stays quiet for the rest of the call. So bring the story, and leave the verdict at home.
